findings.paraphrase: The investigator should follow the randomisation procedures, break the code only in accordance with the protocol, and promptly document and explain to the sponsor any premature unblinding (e.g. accidental, emergency, due to an SAE).
findings.quote: promptly document and explain to the sponsor any premature unblinding
findings.record: documentation and explanation of premature unblinding

reqs.statement: Follow the randomisation procedures, break the code only in accordance with the protocol, and promptly document and explain to the sponsor any premature unblinding.

findings.paraphrase: The principal investigator should have a process (formal SOP or study-specific guidance) ensuring that site staff and service providers delegated by the PI/institution can identify suspected serious breaches and that these are promptly reported to the sponsor or delegated party through the contacts provided.
findings.quote: a (suspected) serious breach is promptly reported to the sponsor or delegated party

reqs.statement: Have a site process that enables site staff and providers delegated by the principal investigator to identify suspected serious breaches and report them promptly to the sponsor or delegated party.
reqs.trigger: Suspected serious breach at the site

Lane assumed: E6(R3) lists this as a monitoring activity under the sponsor's monitoring plan without naming who performs it.
Duty applies to two parties: E6(R3) addresses this data and metadata review to investigators and sponsors; the model shows only the sponsor's review.
Meaning of a term: in E6(R3) 'deviation beyond these ranges' means a range exceedance (e.g. a quality tolerance limit), not a protocol deviation.
Lane assumed: E6(R3) names no performer for this monitoring activity. The requirement names the monitor; 'Who' shows the lane the model uses.
21 CFR 312.62(b) requires case histories recording all observations but does not name deviations; used here as the US basis for site documentation.
Premature unblinding: E6(R3) requires prompt explanation to the sponsor but does not call it a deviation; trial-specific criteria decide whether it is an important deviation.

findings.paraphrase: For Art. 52, a serious breach is a breach likely to affect to a significant degree the safety and rights of a subject or the reliability and robustness of the data generated in the trial. Art. 2 contains no definition of serious breach; this is the only legal definition.
findings.quote: likely to affect to a significant degree the safety and rights of a subject

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: The glossary defines a serious breach as any deviation from the approved protocol version or the clinical trial regulation that is likely to significantly affect participant safety or rights, or data reliability and robustness. There is no separate glossary entry for 'breach'.
findings.quote: Any deviation of the approved protocol version or the clinical trial regulation

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: A suspected serious breach is an incident reported by investigators or service providers that the sponsor has not yet assessed as a serious breach. This defines the intermediate state between identification and sponsor classification.
findings.quote: has not yet been assessed by the sponsor to be a serious breach

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: Only breaches the sponsor has assessed as serious are notified in CTIS; suspected serious breaches are not notified as such. The sponsor classification is the gate before the authority message flow.
findings.quote: only serious breaches must be notified, not suspected serious breaches

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: An important deviation as defined by ICH E3 (Q&A R1) is not equivalent to a serious breach: one does not imply the other, and not every important deviation needs to be reported through CTIS as a serious breach. Two separate classification decisions are needed.
findings.quote: an important deviation is not necessarily also a serious breach and vice versa

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.deadline: within the 7 calendar day notification window for the assessment
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: After receipt, the sponsor assesses whether the breach is serious (deviations/violations, isolated or systematic incidents, participants harmed or put at risk, data credibility) and investigates it, including a root cause analysis that may still be ongoing at the time of reporting.
findings.quote: a root cause analysis

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: Points to consider (bulleted list, not a decision tree): decide whether the breach meets the Art. 52 definition and, if likely significant, regard and report it as serious during the investigation; a proper quality management system should identify the root cause, evaluate the extent and, for a systematic breach, whether other subjects or trials are affected, establish whether human error, lack of training or failure to follow a procedure caused it, and for service-provider causes check the sponsor's other open or closed trials with that provider.

findings.binding_route: EU: EMA training material (non-binding) on implementing EU CTR Art. 52 in CTIS
findings.doc: CTIS Bitesize Talk: End of transition period and notifications including serious breaches, EMA, 16 October 2024 (presentation)
findings.paraphrase: Whether an incident qualifies as a serious breach depends on trial and incident factors and is judged case by case; reporting incidents that are not real serious breaches burdens assessors and should be avoided.
findings.quote: Over-reporting to be avoided!

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022

findings.quote: do not negate the fact that a breach occurred

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52

findings.paraphrase: Example judged a serious breach: a site repeatedly failed, for several subjects over a year and despite monitor findings, to reduce or stop trial medication after abnormal laboratory values as the protocol required. Shows persistence after monitoring escalation as a seriousness factor.

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52

findings.quote: a minor protocol deviation, which does not meet the criteria for notification

findings.paraphrase: Persistent or systematic non-compliance with the Regulation, including deviation from GCP principles or the protocol as described in Art. 47, constitutes a serious breach when it is likely to significantly affect the safety and rights of a participant in the EU/EEA or the reliability and robustness of the trial data. Recurring or trended deviations can therefore escalate to a serious breach.
findings.quote: is likely to significantly affect the safety and rights of a trial participant

reqs.trigger: Pattern of persistent or systematic deviations

reqs.statement: Report every concern about potential fraud that the sponsor becomes aware of as a serious breach.

findings.paraphrase: Information submitted with a notification (mandatory CTIS fields plus free text or uploaded document) covers: A general information (investigation status and next follow-up date, trial title and type, regulatory procedure, other trials impacted with EU CT number, site details, most affected Member State), B breach details (description, potential impact with sub-category, other details) and C actions (impact assessment with methodology, root cause investigation, CAPA plan with owner, timeline, status and how the incident is documented in the TMF, actual impact). Reporting duty not settled: neither E6(R3) nor 21 CFR says whether a protocol deviation that has occurred is a 'change' for prompt IRB/IEC reporting; the model defers to IRB/IEC procedures.
verify_notes: The EMA guideline says 'approved protocol version'; the model uses the EU CTR wording: the protocol version applicable at the time of the breach.
Seven days in EU CTR Art. 52(1) are read as calendar days, as the EMA serious breach guideline states.
E6(R3) gives this duty to the investigator or the sponsor; the model places it with the investigator/institution, who reports changes under the IRB/IEC procedures.
IRB/IEC duties are shown only as message flows from the collapsed IRB/IEC pool; here its reports to FDA and to institutional officials.
21 CFR defines neither 'serious' nor 'continuing' noncompliance, and no source links important protocol deviations to this IRB reporting trigger.
Lane assumed: the source names no reporting party, so periodic deviation reporting is shown in the Sponsor lane.

findings.doc: Oversight of Clinical Investigations - A Risk-Based Approach to Monitoring, Guidance for Industry, August 2013 (final; docket FDA-2011-D-0597)
findings.paraphrase: Sponsors should prospectively identify critical data and processes whose errors would threaten subject protection or trial integrity; examples include verifying that informed consent was properly obtained, adherence to eligibility criteria, investigational product accountability and administration, endpoint and protocol-required safety assessments, serious adverse event reporting, and blinding and allocation concealment.

findings.binding_route: US: FDA draft guidance (Level 1, for comment, nonbinding recommendations); EU: not applicable

findings.paraphrase: Before or during protocol development, sponsors should run a risk assessment to find elements (visit structure, procedures, windows, enrolment criteria) that can be made more flexible or removed, and should identify and document the elements critical to safety and data quality, such as enrolment criteria, safety monitoring and primary or secondary efficacy endpoint procedures.

L4_02_G1.label: Which monitoring channels are due?
notes: Justification: Centralised monitoring can complement and reduce site monitoring or be used on its own (E6R3 A1-3.11.4.2(b)) and site visit frequency follows the risks (A1-3.11.4.1(a)), so one or both channels run in a cycle (FLW-07, DEC-02). Both outgoing flows are conditional and there is no default flow: the trigger 'Monitoring activity scheduled' guarantees at least one channel, and a default flow would wrongly suppress centralised review whenever a site visit is due (an OR default flow runs only when no other condition holds). XOR rejected: the channels are not exclusive.

notes: Justification: Every deviation is reported to the sponsor (A14, before the split: deviation report, FDA-PD24 SIII.B.1, DRAFT, including the premature unblinding explanation, E6R3 A1-2.11). One deviation can in addition require the computerised system incident report (E6R3 A1-2.12.10(e)) and, in the EU, the suspected serious breach report (EMA-SB S6.4); both can apply together (FLW-07, DEC-02). Default flow 'No further report' to the OR join when neither applies.

findings.doc: Protocol Deviations for Clinical Investigations of Drugs, Biological Products, and Devices - Draft Guidance for Industry, December 2024 (CDER, CBER, CDRH, OCE; docket FDA-2023-D-5016)
findings.paraphrase: FDA does not regard every GCP compliance issue as a protocol deviation, particularly where the protocol does not specify the detail (example: a missing signature on a delegation log); counting such issues as deviations inflates numbers. They should be addressed, but outside the protocol deviation process.

findings.binding_route: EU: none (industry best practice); US: none (industry best practice)
findings.doc: Protocol Deviations: A Holistic Approach from Defining to Reporting. Therapeutic Innovation and Regulatory Science 55(4):733-742, 2021 (TransCelerate working group, CC BY 4.0)
findings.page: journal pp. 733-742 (section page not confirmed; PMC HTML read)
findings.paraphrase: To avoid over-counting, an event is treated as a protocol deviation only if three principles hold: it actually happened (not hypothetical), it relates to the protocol or a document the protocol references (e.g. a laboratory manual), and it is judged independent of fault, blame or circumstance. Events failing these tests may need follow-up through other processes.

findings.doc: Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 on clinical trials on medicinal products for human use, OJ L 158, 27.5.2014 (page reference); wording read in EUR-Lex consolidated text 02014R0536-20221205 (05.12.2022)
findings.paraphrase: For Art. 52, a serious breach is a breach likely to affect to a significant degree the safety and rights of a subject or the reliability and robustness of the data generated in the trial. Art. 2 contains no definition of serious breach; this is the only legal definition.
findings.quote: likely to affect to a significant degree the safety and rights of a subject

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: The glossary defines a serious breach as any deviation from the approved protocol version or the clinical trial regulation that is likely to significantly affect participant safety or rights, or data reliability and robustness. There is no separate glossary entry for 'breach'.
findings.quote: Any deviation of the approved protocol version or the clinical trial regulation

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: A suspected serious breach is an incident reported by investigators or service providers that the sponsor has not yet assessed as a serious breach. This defines the intermediate state between identification and sponsor classification.
findings.quote: has not yet been assessed by the sponsor to be a serious breach

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: Only breaches the sponsor has assessed as serious are notified in CTIS; suspected serious breaches are not notified as such. The sponsor classification is the gate before the authority message flow.
findings.quote: only serious breaches must be notified, not suspected serious breaches

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: An important deviation as defined by ICH E3 (Q&A R1) is not equivalent to a serious breach: one does not imply the other, and not every important deviation needs to be reported through CTIS as a serious breach. Two separate classification decisions are needed.
findings.quote: an important deviation is not necessarily also a serious breach and vice versa

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.deadline: within the 7 calendar day notification window for the assessment
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: After receipt, the sponsor assesses whether the breach is serious (deviations/violations, isolated or systematic incidents, participants harmed or put at risk, data credibility) and investigates it, including a root cause analysis that may still be ongoing at the time of reporting.
findings.quote: a root cause analysis

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: Points to consider (bulleted list, not a decision tree): decide whether the breach meets the Art. 52 definition and, if likely significant, regard and report it as serious during the investigation; a proper quality management system should identify the root cause, evaluate the extent and, for a systematic breach, whether other subjects or trials are affected, establish whether human error, lack of training or failure to follow a procedure caused it, and for service-provider causes check the sponsor's other open or closed trials with that provider.

findings.binding_route: EU: EMA training material (non-binding) on implementing EU CTR Art. 52 in CTIS
findings.doc: CTIS Bitesize Talk: End of transition period and notifications including serious breaches, EMA, 16 October 2024 (presentation)
findings.paraphrase: Whether an incident qualifies as a serious breach depends on trial and incident factors and is judged case by case; reporting incidents that are not real serious breaches burdens assessors and should be avoided.
findings.quote: Over-reporting to be avoided!

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: Corrective or remedial actions taken do not change the fact that a breach occurred; mitigation is not a reason to skip classification or notification. Systematic or significant mis-dosing meets the criteria whether or not adverse reactions occurred.
findings.quote: do not negate the fact that a breach occurred

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: Example judged a serious breach: a site repeatedly failed, for several subjects over a year and despite monitor findings, to reduce or stop trial medication after abnormal laboratory values as the protocol required. Shows persistence after monitoring escalation as a seriousness factor.

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: Example judged not a serious breach: a common, minor visit date deviation is a minor protocol deviation that does not meet the notification criteria; a major visit date deviation (8.3) can be serious depending on its safety or data impact.
findings.quote: a minor protocol deviation, which does not meet the criteria for notification

reqs.statement: Assess each potential breach of EU CTR or of the protocol version applicable at the time against the serious breach definition (likely to affect to a significant degree the safety and rights of a subject or the reliability and robustness of the data), as a decision separate from the iPD classification, and notify only breaches assessed as serious.
reqs.trigger: Sponsor becomes aware of a potential breach
verify_notes: The EMA guideline says 'approved protocol version'; the model uses the EU CTR wording: the protocol version applicable at the time of the breach.
verify_raw: [verify] EMA-SB glossary refers to the 'approved protocol version', Art. 52(1) to the version applicable at the time of the breach (C-14)

reqs.action: Assess breach impact on data reliability
reqs.binding_route: EMA-SB: EMA guideline interpreting EU CTR Art. 52 (non-binding guidance)

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: Whether a breach significantly affects data reliability depends on factors such as trial design, the type and extent of affected data, their contribution to key analyses and the impact of excluding them. These are CtQ-like assessment criteria.

reqs.statement: Judge whether a breach significantly affects data reliability by the trial design, the type and extent of the affected data, their contribution to key analyses and the impact of excluding them.

reqs.action: Assess persistent noncompliance as serious breach
reqs.binding_route: EMA-SB: EMA guideline interpreting EU CTR Art. 52 (non-binding guidance)

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: Persistent or systematic non-compliance with the Regulation, including deviation from GCP principles or the protocol as described in Art. 47, constitutes a serious breach when it is likely to significantly affect the safety and rights of a participant in the EU/EEA or the reliability and robustness of the trial data. Recurring or trended deviations can therefore escalate to a serious breach.
findings.quote: is likely to significantly affect the safety and rights of a trial participant

reqs.statement: Treat persistent or systematic non-compliance with the Regulation, GCP principles or the protocol as a serious breach when it is likely to significantly affect participants in the EU/EEA or the reliability and robustness of the data.
reqs.trigger: Pattern of persistent or systematic deviations

reqs.action: Report potential fraud as serious breach
reqs.binding_route: EMA-SB: EMA guideline interpreting EU CTR Art. 52 (non-binding guidance)

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: All concerns about potential fraud in clinical trials that the sponsor becomes aware of are expected to be reported as serious breaches; national criminal law applies in addition.
findings.quote: all concerns about potential cases of fraud in clinical trials

reqs.statement: Report every concern about potential fraud that the sponsor becomes aware of as a serious breach.

reqs.binding_route: EMA-SB: EMA guideline interpreting EU CTR Art. 52 (non-binding guidance)

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: A breach (e.g. mis-dosing from an error) that may result in an SAE or SUSAR can be a serious breach, and failure to manage safety events (e.g. lack of SUSAR reporting) that puts participants at significant risk is a serious breach to be reported; this does not exempt the sponsor from Art. 53/54 notifications or EudraVigilance SUSAR submission.

reqs.statement: Treat a breach that may result in an SAE or SUSAR, or a failure to manage safety events that puts participants at significant risk, as a serious breach, without replacing the EU CTR Art. 53/54 notifications or SUSAR reporting.

reqs.binding_route: EMA-SB: EMA guideline interpreting EU CTR Art. 52 (non-binding guidance)

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: A serious breach at a single site, inside or outside the EU/EEA, should also be notified where it leads to removal of data from the trial analysis.
findings.quote: this leads to the removal of data from the trial analysis

reqs.statement: Notify a serious breach at a single site, inside or outside the EU/EEA, where it leads to removal of data from the trial analysis.
reqs.trigger: Site-level breach causing data exclusion from analysis

reqs.binding_route: EMA-SB: EMA guideline interpreting EU CTR Art. 52 (non-binding guidance)

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: It is the sponsor's responsibility to perform a thorough root cause analysis and to assess the impact of the breach on data reliability and robustness and on participant safety and/or rights; this assessment should be documented, as the sponsor's decisions may be examined later, e.g. during GCP inspections.

reqs.statement: Perform and document a thorough root cause analysis and an assessment of the breach's impact on data reliability and on participant safety and rights, so that the sponsor's decision can be examined later, for example in GCP inspections.

reqs.binding_route: EUCTR: Regulation (EU) No 536/2014, directly applicable in all EU Member States

findings.binding_route: EU: directly applicable regulation
findings.doc: Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 on clinical trials on medicinal products for human use, OJ L 158, 27.5.2014 (page reference); wording read in EUR-Lex consolidated text 02014R0536-20221205 (05.12.2022)
findings.paraphrase: For Art. 52, a serious breach is a breach likely to affect to a significant degree the safety and rights of a subject or the reliability and robustness of the data generated in the trial. Art. 2 contains no definition of serious breach; this is the only legal definition.
findings.quote: likely to affect to a significant degree the safety and rights of a subject

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: The glossary defines a serious breach as any deviation from the approved protocol version or the clinical trial regulation that is likely to significantly affect participant safety or rights, or data reliability and robustness. There is no separate glossary entry for 'breach'.
findings.quote: Any deviation of the approved protocol version or the clinical trial regulation

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: A suspected serious breach is an incident reported by investigators or service providers that the sponsor has not yet assessed as a serious breach. This defines the intermediate state between identification and sponsor classification.
findings.quote: has not yet been assessed by the sponsor to be a serious breach

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: Only breaches the sponsor has assessed as serious are notified in CTIS; suspected serious breaches are not notified as such. The sponsor classification is the gate before the authority message flow.
findings.quote: only serious breaches must be notified, not suspected serious breaches

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: An important deviation as defined by ICH E3 (Q&A R1) is not equivalent to a serious breach: one does not imply the other, and not every important deviation needs to be reported through CTIS as a serious breach. Two separate classification decisions are needed.
findings.quote: an important deviation is not necessarily also a serious breach and vice versa

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.deadline: within the 7 calendar day notification window for the assessment
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: After receipt, the sponsor assesses whether the breach is serious (deviations/violations, isolated or systematic incidents, participants harmed or put at risk, data credibility) and investigates it, including a root cause analysis that may still be ongoing at the time of reporting.
findings.quote: a root cause analysis

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: Points to consider (bulleted list, not a decision tree): decide whether the breach meets the Art. 52 definition and, if likely significant, regard and report it as serious during the investigation; a proper quality management system should identify the root cause, evaluate the extent and, for a systematic breach, whether other subjects or trials are affected, establish whether human error, lack of training or failure to follow a procedure caused it, and for service-provider causes check the sponsor's other open or closed trials with that provider.

findings.binding_route: EU: EMA training material (non-binding) on implementing EU CTR Art. 52 in CTIS
findings.doc: CTIS Bitesize Talk: End of transition period and notifications including serious breaches, EMA, 16 October 2024 (presentation)
findings.paraphrase: Whether an incident qualifies as a serious breach depends on trial and incident factors and is judged case by case; reporting incidents that are not real serious breaches burdens assessors and should be avoided.
findings.quote: Over-reporting to be avoided!

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: Corrective or remedial actions taken do not change the fact that a breach occurred; mitigation is not a reason to skip classification or notification. Systematic or significant mis-dosing meets the criteria whether or not adverse reactions occurred.
findings.quote: do not negate the fact that a breach occurred

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: Example judged a serious breach: a site repeatedly failed, for several subjects over a year and despite monitor findings, to reduce or stop trial medication after abnormal laboratory values as the protocol required. Shows persistence after monitoring escalation as a seriousness factor.

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: Example judged not a serious breach: a common, minor visit date deviation is a minor protocol deviation that does not meet the notification criteria; a major visit date deviation (8.3) can be serious depending on its safety or data impact.
findings.quote: a minor protocol deviation, which does not meet the criteria for notification

reqs.action: Notify serious breach via EU portal
reqs.binding_route: EUCTR: Regulation (EU) No 536/2014, directly applicable in all EU Member States
reqs.deadline: without undue delay, at the latest 7 (calendar) days from sponsor awareness of the potential breach

findings.binding_route: EU: directly applicable regulation
findings.deadline: without undue delay but not later than seven days of becoming aware of that breach
findings.doc: Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 on clinical trials on medicinal products for human use, OJ L 158, 27.5.2014 (page reference); wording read in EUR-Lex consolidated text 02014R0536-20221205 (05.12.2022)
findings.paraphrase: The sponsor must notify the Member States concerned, through the EU portal, of a serious breach of the Regulation or of the protocol version applicable at the time of the breach, without undue delay and at the latest seven days after becoming aware of it. The clock starts at sponsor awareness.
findings.quote: the version of the protocol applicable at the time of the breach

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.deadline: without undue delay and at the latest within 7 calendar days of the sponsor becoming aware
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: The notification is due without undue delay and at the latest within 7 calendar days of the sponsor becoming aware; the sponsor should perform any assessment needed to confirm seriousness in a timely manner, and that assessment should not extend the 7-day period (the 7-day limit itself is binding through EU CTR Art. 52(1)).
findings.quote: within 7 calendar days of the sponsor becoming aware of a serious breach

findings.binding_route: EU: Commission/CTAG Q&A (non-binding) interpreting EU CTR
findings.deadline: within seven days of becoming aware of the potential breach
findings.doc: Clinical Trials Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 Questions & Answers, EudraLex Volume 10, version 7.4, October 2026 (supersedes 7.3)
findings.paraphrase: Q&A 11.3 (point 523): the 7-day timeframe of Art. 52(1) starts when the sponsor becomes aware of a potential breach; only confirmed serious breaches are reported, so the sponsor completes its first analysis, confirms seriousness and submits the initial report in CTIS within those 7 days.
findings.quote: The 7-day timeframe starts when the sponsor becomes aware of a potential breach.

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: Where the sponsor has reasonable, evidence-based grounds to believe a serious breach occurred, it should notify first and continue investigating in parallel, without waiting for all details.
findings.quote: should not wait to obtain all of the details

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: The sponsor is responsible for the serious breach notification via the EU portal / CTIS and may delegate the task to a service provider by written agreement as described in EU CTR Art. 71, while keeping responsibility.
findings.quote: may delegate this task to a service provider

findings.binding_route: EU: Commission/CTAG Q&A (non-binding) interpreting EU CTR
findings.doc: Clinical Trials Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 Questions & Answers, EudraLex Volume 10, version 7.4, October 2026 (supersedes 7.3)
findings.page: printed 4-5 (chapter 1; page numbers restart per chapter)
findings.paraphrase: Q&A 1.5: all submissions for a trial, including site information, are made by or on behalf of the sponsor, not the investigator, via CTIS or EudraVigilance. Investigators therefore do not notify authorities directly under the EU CTR.

findings.binding_route: EU: EMA training material (non-binding) on implementing EU CTR Art. 52 in CTIS
findings.doc: CTIS Bitesize Talk: End of transition period and notifications including serious breaches, EMA, 16 October 2024 (presentation)
findings.page: slide 20; notification type label on an unnumbered CTCG slide
findings.paraphrase: For trials authorised in the EU/EEA, a serious breach is reported via CTIS to all Member States concerned regardless of where it occurred; the notification type is 'Serious Breaches, safety relevant (SB)'.
findings.quote: the SB should be reported via CTIS to all MSC

reqs.statement: Notify a serious breach to the Member States concerned through the EU portal without undue delay and at the latest seven days after becoming aware of it (EU CTR Art. 52(1)); per EMA and Commission guidance the period runs from awareness of the potential breach, the sponsor should assess seriousness in a timely manner without extending the period, and where there are reasonable grounds it should notify first and continue investigating.
reqs.trigger: Sponsor becomes aware of a potential serious breach
verify: Deadline not settled: the sources start the EU 7-day serious breach clock at sponsor awareness but do not say whether awareness of a delegated party, CRO or monitor counts.
verify_notes: Seven days in EU CTR Art. 52(1) are read as calendar days, as the EMA serious breach guideline states.
verify_raw: [verify] whose awareness (delegated party, CRO, monitor) starts the clock is not defined (C-05)
[verify] 'seven days' (Art. 52(1)) read as calendar days per EMA-SB S3.2 (C-13)

reqs.binding_route: EMA-SB: EMA guideline interpreting EU CTR Art. 52 (non-binding guidance); CTIS-BT-SB24: EMA CTIS training material (non-binding guidance); CTIS-TM17: EMA CTIS training material (non-binding guidance)
reqs.deadline: none (no assessment timeline set in law, per CTIS-BT-SB24 slide 29)

findings.binding_route: EU: non-binding guideline (CTFG and GCP IWG), implements EU CTR Art. 52
findings.deadline: none (no assessment timeline set in law, per CTIS-BT-SB24 slide 29)
findings.doc: Guideline for the notification of serious breaches of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 or the clinical trial protocol, EMA/698382/2021, document date 30 June 2023, effective 31 January 2022
findings.paraphrase: Member States assess notified serious breaches in the CTIS secure module; the assessment leads to publication of the breach and its evaluation in the CTIS public domain. Some breaches are managed in-house through acceptable CAPA under Member State oversight; others may trigger an (urgent) inspection, published together with the inspection report, or regulatory action.
findings.quote: managed in-house via acceptable Corrective and Preventive Actions

findings.binding_route: EU: EMA training material (non-binding) on CTIS transparency for EU CTR Art. 52 notifications
findings.doc: CTIS Bitesize Talk: End of transition period and notifications including serious breaches, EMA, 16 October 2024 (presentation)
findings.paraphrase: Serious breach, USM and unexpected event notifications are published only after the Member State assessment is finalised in CTIS (for Category 1 trials in adults: 30 months after EU/EEA end of trial and MSC assessment). Only sponsor-entered structured data are published, no authority-entered data and no notification documents; a serious breach withdrawn at Member State request is not published.
findings.quote: The notification is published only once the Member State assessment is finalized in CTIS

findings.binding_route: EU: EMA CTIS training material (non-binding), authority-side handling
findings.doc: Supervise a CT - Ad Hoc Assessment: FAQs, CTIS Training Programme Module 17, version 1.3, August 2024 (EMA)
findings.paraphrase: Member States may create an ad hoc assessment in CTIS linked to serious breach, urgent safety measure or unexpected event notifications; the outcome is informative only and a change of trial status requires a recommended action such as a corrective measure. Sponsors take part only if RFIs are raised.
findings.party: MSs (represented by NCAs and Ethics Committees)

findings.binding_route: EU: EMA CTIS training material (non-binding), authority-side handling
findings.doc: Supervise a CT - Ad Hoc Assessment: FAQs, CTIS Training Programme Module 17, version 1.3, August 2024 (EMA)
findings.paraphrase: When finalising, the Member State links the assessment conclusion to the notification or selects 'no Ad-hoc assessment required'; either action publishes the notification details on the CTIS public portal.

reqs.reason: Authority-side process inside the collapsed Regulatory authority pool.
reqs.statement: Member States assess serious breach and urgent safety measure notifications in CTIS (ad hoc assessment) and publish them after assessment.
